It refuses a duplicate or an out-of-order section number now, and the file runs in sequence again. A colour in the checker had drifted from the stylesheet. --cedar was lightened so a drawing’s outline would pass, and check-contrast.py kept the old value — so one pair in that file spent a commit measuring a colour that was no longer on the site. It is fixed, and every run now prints which colours declared in:root the checker has never heard of. There are thirteen, all pre-existing; they are reported rather than refused, because some are genuinely decorative and one is a variable nothing uses at all, and a checker that blocks a deploy on somebody else’s unfinished decision is the wrong shape. The three chairs have something on each of them, and each names a real entry in our glossary. Stimming, parallel play — being alone together, which is what three chairs and one screen and no obligation actually is — and stim-watching, which is Jim Irion’s term and his account, and is the reason nobody here will ask why you have put the hummingbirds on for the fourth time. Two of the three carry somebody else’s words and say so on the chair.

item.title: three benches in the Hermitage, and a check that stopped guessing at Latin
item.description: The watering hole is open, which finishes the room. Three tables pushed together under the long window: a herbarium, a solar bench, and a table of Star Stuff. A watering hole is where you learn from the people next to you, so nothing on these benches is a lesson — it is somebody else’s work left out where you can pick it up. One room, three postures, and that is what keeps the three zones apart. The cave is enclosed, round-cornered and dark and you are sitting in it. The campfire is seated too, and its cards are rounded because a bean bag has no corners. The workshop is flat-topped and square — worktops with a lip at the front, things laid out on them, and you are standing up. Every specimen in the herbarium is there because one of our own pages argues from it, and make-hermitage.py refuses one that is not. Dandelion, tulip and orchid off the sensitivity metaphor; a bamboo rhizome for Helen Edgar’s Autistic Rhizome; a fern frond because it is the picture our glossary reaches for to explain a fractal; moss, lichen, mycelium and an envelope with nothing in it, off four Star Stuff pieces. There is no sunflower, although sunflowers are the plant growing outside the door — we have no page about them, so there is nothing to press, and the table says so. Nothing in it is named to species, and the check that enforces that had to be thrown away and rewritten. A Latin binomial typed from memory is a taxonomic claim nobody checked, wearing the one kind of authority a herbarium sheet has. The first version looked for Latin endings — and missed Taraxacum officinale, the single most likely binomial to end up on this table, then missed two more after two rounds of widening, while every widening walked it closer to firing on ordinary prose. A tripwire that is allowed to miss and at risk of crying wolf is the worst of both. So the shape is the check now and the English words are the allowlist: a name of one capitalised word and one lowercase word is refused unless the second word is one this table has declared. That catches every binomial rather than the ones somebody anticipated, and it costs one word added on purpose when a plain name like fern frond arrives. All of this was found by putting a binomial in on purpose, which is the only reason any of it is known. The solar bench is books and videos about the thing on the roof. The videos came off our own Solarpunk entry and the reading off our own Electrify Everything — which is the only item on any of these three tables that we wrote. Every id was checked on its own watch page and every title and channel resolved against YouTube rather than taken from our link text, which mattered here: our glossary credits the first of them as “ft. @Andrewism”, and the channel that published it is Our Changing Climate. Two different facts, and only one of them was written down. Griffith’s Electrify is the second id in this file resolved by search rather than lifted, for the same reason Care Work was, and it was requested and answered before it went up. Twice in one room is a pattern rather than an accident: our pages name an author far more often than they link a book. The Star Stuff table refuses anything that does not point at starstuff.earth. A bench with somebody’s name on it holding something else is a mis-filed thing that reads as a claim. Six pieces, all linked out and none reproduced — including A Field Guide to the Ways of Being Alone, which says a lone wolf is not an outcast but a disperser, and is the keystone of this whole pitch arriving from the sibling site rather than from us. Three of the herbarium’s sheets come off pieces on the third table, and they say so. That is what a workshop with three benches in one room looks like, and it is the argument for putting them in one room rather than three. Nine new contrast pairs, including the first ground on this street that is a lighter card on a darker surface — a pressed sheet laid on a worktop, which is the opposite way round from every card here. 338 pairs, none failing.

item.title: the first daylit room on the street, and a laptop that frames the street inside it
item.description: The Solarpunk Hermitage is open, on pitch 03 at the far end of the campgrounds. Ryan’s own place: a wood cabin on wheels bristling with panels, sunflowers taller than the door, an aerial going up out of the quiet. It is daylit, and that is the whole of its separation from everything else here. Every other world on this street is a dark ground with light put on it — neon on black, candle on canvas, lamp on earth, a screen in a dark arcade, shafts through a canopy. This one is the morning. A cabin that runs on the sun and reads as midnight would be an argument against itself, and the panels on that roof are the reason the lamp in the cave never gutters. It also means the arrival works twice in opposite directions: out of the field’s cold dusk into a lit tent at pitch 01, and out of the same dusk into full sun at pitch 03. The cave, the campfire and the watering hole are David Thornburg’s and are named as his. They are the primordial learning spaces from From the Campfire to the Holodeck, which our own glossary documents: the cave is where you learn from yourself, the campfire is where you learn from a storyteller, the watering hole is where you learn from peers. Taking a framework’s shape and not its author’s name is the failure this site keeps attribution for. There is a fourth, Life, where you make something out of what the other three gave you; the room says out loud that it is not in here, it is the door you came in by. And the argument the pitch stands on is Betsy Selvam’s. Lone wolfing is being alone well rather than being left out, and that distinction is hers, credited by name in the room and in the liner notes, not folded into our “we”. The cave is the hardest room this street has had to keep apart from its neighbours. It is the fourth warm enclosed space here, after the Faery Yurt, The Latibulum and The Den — and “it is a cosy reading nook, it should feel like the other cosy places” is the Latibulum argument arriving a second time, which is exactly when it stops sounding wrong. Three structural things keep it: the other three are each lit by one flickering source in the dark and this one is evenly lit at reading brightness, with the candles as ornaments on a room that does not need them; the others are canvas, earth and panelling and this is textile, with no wood and no straight edge in it but the shelves; and you reach the others out of the cold, while you reach this one out of full daylight and it is darker than where you came from. Every book on those shelves is one we already argue from, and each says which page of ours put it there — read out of the Knowledge System mirror’s own frontmatter rather than typed. Butler, Baldwin, Thornburg, brown, Kropotkin, Piepzna-Samarasinha, Chapman, Totton, Silberman, Kelly. A borrow link is required and a buy link is not, and make-hermitage.py refuses a spine without one: our library page says knowledge is infrastructure and access to it is mutual aid, and a shelf that could only tell you where to buy would be a shop with an argument painted on it. One of those ids was assembled from memory and was wrong, in the file whose own header says not to do that. Care Work is the one book our pages link without an Open Library id, and the id written for it pointed at a different work entirely. It was caught by checking, resolved against Open Library’s search, and the whole episode is written into the data file rather than quietly corrected — every borrow and buy link in there was then requested and answered before any of it went up. The campfire is Ryan’s list of documentaries and nothing on it was chosen in this repo. Every id was checked on its own watch page — status, embeddability and length — and every title and channel was resolved against YouTube rather than typed off the links that arrived. Every button says how long it runs before you press it, and make-hermitage.py refuses one without a runtime, which is the exact inverse of make-jungle.py refusing a cam that has one. A live camera has no length to give and a film does; the two tools keep the same promise and must not be made to agree. One of the twelve plays and cannot be embedded, which is the Jungle Room’s lesson arriving in a new room from a new list. It is published as a door out rather than a screen, shaped like a door so it does not promise a picture it cannot show, and saying why on its own face. Its title and channel came off the watch page, because YouTube’s oEmbed refuses it too. The laptop in the cave frames stimpunks.love inside stimpunks.love, and it is the real street — you can walk down it from in there. It still waits to be pressed, for a different reason than the jukebox facades: nothing third-party is involved, but a whole copy of the street loading itself unasked means a second intensity dial underneath the first, every font served twice, and a screen reader walking the entire site again for somebody who came in to read a book. And it refuses to nest. A laptop showing the street is a laptop you can walk back into this room through, and the third one is not a joke any more — it is a page that will not stop loading and an accessibility tree nobody can get out of. A hermitage that finds itself already inside a frame says one screen is enough instead of offering the laptop. The security header had to change for any of that, and it is the only loosening in the policy. frame-ancestors was 'none', which forbids this site being framed by anybody, itself included, and X-Frame-Options was DENY. They are 'self' and SAMEORIGIN now. Clickjacking protection against every other origin is unchanged; what is permitted is exactly one page of ours embedding another page of ours, after a press. The reasoning is in _headers and in tools/make-csp.py beside the line that generates it. The contrast checker had to learn a room that is dark on light. This is the first one on the street whose type sits on a bright ground all the way down, which inverts the usual failure: the dangerous inks here are the pale accents rather than the dim greys. It refused three things before the room shipped — the cabin’s outline on its own timber, the leaves drawn on the ground band, and a sunflower held to the wrong threshold — and it also caught a collision in its own source, where the new room’s green was named LEAF and silently overwrote The Chappell’s gold, failing five of that room’s pairs. A checker catching a bug in itself is the argument for having it. 329 pairs, none failing. Two faces nothing else here sets, because no two rooms on this street share a voice. Fraunces swells and curls; Sora is drawn on a grid with flat terminals. Tech and nature, set in type, rather than one of them in fancy dress. The watering hole has its benches in and nothing laid out on them. A herbarium, a solar bench and a table of Star Stuff, marked as what they are rather than hidden until they are ready — the same honesty the empty storefront and the zine’s empty line use.

item.title: two drawings on the campground’s board, and a pitch taken at the far end
item.description: The field’s pitches have pictures on them now. A yurt sat against the trees with its doorway lit, and a wood cabin on wheels bristling with solar panels. They are what you can see of each pitch from the gate, which is what the board has said it is for since the field opened: read the sign before you go in. An open plot has no drawing at all, and that is the whole grammar rather than an omission. What is pitched is what you can see from here; bare ground looks like bare ground. They are signs, not rooms, which is the only reason two of them may sit on one board. Both are drawn in the field’s own inks — spruce and bark for the masses, moss for every line, weight rather than tint doing the hierarchy — because you are looking at them across cold ground at night. Neither one is a preview of the world inside it, and neither one may become one. What tells them apart is one lit colour each, and the two lights do opposite things. The yurt emits: candle amber out of the crown, out of the doorway and onto the grass in front of it, round and soft-edged and strung with lights. The hermitage catches: nothing on it glows except one window, the moon lands on its panels, three sunflowers hold the only warm colour on the pitch, and the aerial is the one line reaching off it. Round and warm against angular and cool. The rule for the next pitch is written beside them in love.css: the field’s inks, one light of its own, and not either of those two lights, because they are taken. And that one window is a screen rather than a flame, which is the pitch’s argument in the only place a drawing can make it. Lone wolfing is not being unreachable; it is choosing the reach. A hermitage lit by a candle would have been a nicer picture and a different idea. Nothing in either drawing moves, at any setting, like everything else out here. The yurt’s fairy lights twinkle on its own page and are still on the board, because this is the field’s drawing of the tent and not the tent. Pitch 03 is taken and has no door yet. The Solarpunk Hermitage, Ryan’s, at the far end — which is where the board already said it was for the people whose whole specification is distance from the street. It is a post with a sign and a drawing and no link, because a campground has that state and a website usually pretends it does not. The honest alternative was publishing a room before it was a room. The card stopped listing the pitches by hand. make-og.py had the plots typed into a string literal, and again into the alt text, in the file whose entire argument is that a card must not be able to disagree with its page. It reads them off the board’s own posts now — middots on the card, commas in the alt text, because a screen reader reads a middot out loud — and refuses to build a field with no plots in it. The drawings are measured, because WCAG does not reach them. The canopy in the Jungle Room is why: it came in at 2.18 against the ground behind it, a smudge with no telling one leaf from another, and nothing was looking. Ten new pairs — every line against open ground and against the ground band, both lit colours against the mass they sit on, the dark disc inside a sunflower, the glazing bars on that screen. 294 in the file, none failing. Holding one ink at one threshold is why there are ten and not thirty: a ladder of dimmer greens would each have needed arguing about. The drawing of Helen’s yurt is ours and is said to be. It is the field’s sign for her pitch, in the field’s inks, seen from outside in the dark; it changes nothing on her page. That is written into the liner notes beside her credit rather than left to be inferred, for the same reason the one colour of hers this site changed is written down in four places.

item.title: a door at the back of the Jungle Room, and the other Jungle Room behind it
item.description: The Den is open, and it is an easter egg. There is no door for it on the street. The way in is a quiet line at the foot of the Jungle Room — the same shape as the door through to The Chappell, turned right down: a hairline, small type and the room’s dimmest ink, below everything else in the room. You find it by getting to the bottom. Quiet is a visual setting and not a perceptual one. That door is an ordinary focusable link with real words in it, in the tab order, at full size, read out by a screen reader like anything else on the street. On a Disabled people’s site a secret only a sighted mouse user can find is not a secret, it is an exclusion, so the floor is written into the stylesheet beside the rule: nothing hidden, no one-pixel target, no display:none. It is Graceland’s Jungle Room, which is a real room and a better joke than the pun. Elvis Presley’s den: Polynesian furniture bought after Blue Hawaii, fur over the seats, an indoor waterfall of cut field stone on the north wall, and a green shag carpet. People have been rude about it for fifty years. And in 1976 it was converted into a recording studio, and the bulk of his last two albums came out of it — From Elvis Presley Boulevard, Memphis, Tennessee and Moody Blue. That fact is what turns a pun into a room: a carpet is a joke, a discography made on top of one is a listening bench. Sixteen cuts, in the order they were recorded, with the night each one was made. Twelve from the February week and four from the three nights in October, ending on the last studio session of his life. The track list, the session dates, the songwriters and the album attributions came off the two albums’ own articles. Nothing was guessed and nothing was typed from memory. Each title was searched on YouTube, the candidates filtered to Presley’s official channels, and every id then checked on its own watch page — channel, playability, embeddability, length. Twelve are on the estate’s art-track channel and four on his VEVO. And every runtime was matched against the released one, because searching any of these turns up alternate takes on the same official channels: a room whose argument is these are the records that came out of that carpet cannot quietly hand somebody a rehearsal. The writers are named on every cut. Presley wrote none of these songs. Gatlin, Sedaka and Cody, Mark James, Dennis Linde, Fred Rose, Layng Martine Jr., Lloyd Webber and Rice, and the rest. A room that credited only the voice would be doing the one thing this site keeps attribution for, in the room where the performer’s name is the entire draw. Every button says how long it runs, and that is the parent’s rule inverted rather than broken. make-jungle.py refuses a runtime because a live camera never ends; make-den.py refuses a track without one because a song has a length and withholding it keeps back the thing that lets somebody decide. Two generators, opposite checks, one promise. Read them together. The hardest subroom yet, because this one shares its parent’s name and its parent’s colour. The Chappell at least did not sound like Pink Pony Club. So the split is structural and stated: upstairs the green is the darkness and the light falls from above; down here the room is brown, the carpet is the brightest thing in it, and the track list is set dark on the green. Same hue, opposite job. One is outdoors, open and has no straight edge in it; this is low, closed and rectangular, full of carved frames with the corners notched out. One sets a serif whose strokes swell as they curve; this sets a slab with no contrast in it at all, because one is a botanical plate and the other is a record sleeve from 1976. The share cards invert too, and had to. Its parent’s card is a dark green field with a roof of leaves and light coming down. This one is a brown panelled wall with a slab of bright shag across the foot and the type dark on it. If the two had not inverted, splitting them into separate cards would have bought nothing. And the contrast checker caught the thing the eye does not. A track card is a pane of cream at 78% laid on the shag, so the type on it sits on what those two make and not on the green — measured against the carpet it would have been measuring a ground no word in the room is actually on. The composite lesson again, arriving in the place it is easiest to miss, because the carpet is the thing you see. Twenty-seven new pairs, 284 in the file, none failing.

item.title: the critter cam comes back as a door, not a window
item.description: Ryan sent a replacement for CritterVision’s Critter Cam, and it is not dead. The new id answers OK and was live when it was checked — but playableInEmbed is false, on the same channel id as the one it replaces, with oEmbed refusing it with a 401 the same way. CritterVision has embedding switched off across the channel, so no id from them would come out differently. It is published as a way out to YouTube rather than as a screen that would show a refusal where the picture should be. Which is the distinction that room was built around, arriving from outside it. Playing and embedding are two different permissions, and the obvious assumption — a working replacement is an embeddable one — is wrong here. The check is one line and it is now written into CLAUDE.md beside the rule about not picking ids from this repo. Nothing in the room is dark. Both cams that answered UNPLAYABLE have come back from the events page, both were measured before they went up, and both entries carry a replaced note saying what was measured. The jelly cam came back as a screen and the critter cam came back as a link, which is the honest difference between them. A door does not get pressed, either. Every plate in the room ended pressing is what sends the request, which is true of a screen and false of a link-out — following one is. It is generated per state now, and the three notes stopped repeating what the door already says on its own face. And the note in the room had to learn to say that. With nothing dark it said only that every cam is playing — true, and it would have let a reader assume they could all be opened here. It counts the link-outs in the same breath now. That is the second time in two days this paragraph has been wrong about its own grammar: the number word and the noun were glued into one lookup, so the first build of this sentence published “Three cams of them”. Two maps now, and both branches agree with their own counts.

item.title: the jelly cam comes back, and a generated number with hand-written grammar around it
item.description: The Live Jelly Cam is in the Jungle Room again. Ryan sent a new id the same day the old one was found dead, which is the process working exactly as DECISIONS.md said it should: the ids on the events page are his, a replacement chosen in this repo would have been a cam nobody chose, and this one came from the person who curates the list. It was checked before it went up. oEmbed returns the same title and the same channel, the watch page answers OK, and playableInEmbed is true — so it is the same cam under a new stream rather than a different thing with a familiar name. That is written into the entry as a replaced note, because a replacement nobody checked is the original bug with a fresh id on it. CritterVision’s Critter Cam is still dark, and the room now says so in the singular without anybody editing a paragraph. Which turned up a small thing worth keeping. The room’s note about dead cams generates its count, for the reason check-counts.py exists — and it generated the count while leaving the rest of the sentence plural, so one dead cam read as “One cam … has gone dark … The entries are … Replacing them”. A generated number in front of hand-written grammar is a sentence that goes wrong the moment the number changes, which is a hand-typed total wearing a better disguise. The whole sentence agrees now. The same edit went through the liner notes, which had the count typed out in full.

item.title: a viewing room under a canopy, and the one facade on this street that must not say how long it runs
item.description: The Jungle Room is open. A door on the street that opens under a closed roof of leaves: light coming down in shafts, and screens cut into the shape of the gaps. Every screen is somebody else’s camera pointed at somewhere real, and every one of them is off until you open it. Ryan’s brief. The cams are our own events page’s, and so is the order they are in. Our Watering Hole Hangs puts one of these up in the background every weekday — no slides, no presenter, no outcomes — and this room is that list, in that page’s own groups and that page’s own sequence. It is a list somebody keeps, not one for this street to re-sort. The ids came off the hrefs, read out of the Knowledge System mirror rather than fetched live, because on stimpunks.org a 301 is a failure and not a pass. The train cams are deliberately not here: a cab view down a Norwegian line is a fine thing to hang about in and it is not a watering hole. And this is the one room on the street where a runtime would be the dishonest thing. Every other press-to-play control here says how long it runs before you press it, and make-latibulum.py refuses a track without one, because that number is what lets somebody decide. A live camera has no runtime. The reflex arriving from three other data files is to store the length of whichever stream happens to be up today, which is a number that is wrong tomorrow and looks authoritative in the meantime — so make-jungle.py refuses a cam that has one, which is the exact inverse of the burrow’s check and the same promise. The label says the true thing instead: it runs until you close it. And the room says out loud that the picture may be darkness, rain, an empty waterhole, or a cam between streams, because a camera pointed at somewhere real is often pointed at nothing, and sitting with nothing happening is most of what the room is for. Playing and embedding turned out to be two different permissions, and nothing here knew that. love-embed.js checks that an id is well-formed and builds an iframe; it cannot know that the video’s owner has switched embedding off. The frame loads and shows a refusal where the picture should be — a button somebody presses and presses that never becomes a video, which is the failure make-chappell.py exists to prevent, arriving through a door no checker was watching. Two of these cams are like that. They get a way out to YouTube, dressed as a door rather than as a window, saying why. check-jukebox.py reads playableInEmbed off the same fetch as the status now, for every facade on the street, and a cam already published as a link-out is not reported. Two cams on our own published events page are dead, and that page does not know it. Monterey Bay Aquarium’s Live Jelly Cam and CritterVision’s Critter Cam both answer UNPLAYABLE. They render nothing here and the room says so in its own copy, with their names in it, because a gallery quietly shorter than the page it came from is this site correcting a published page by deleting the evidence. The entries stay in the data file with the date they were found dead on. Replacing them is a curation decision on the events page and not one this street gets to make on its own — Ryan’s call. Nothing was typed off our own link text. Every title and every channel was resolved against YouTube’s oEmbed endpoint, and the three ids oEmbed refuses were read off the watch page’s own owner name. None of these cameras is ours; attribution is the one careful habit this street kept, and a credit taken from a link somebody wrote by hand is a guess wearing a citation. It is night-green under a roof, next to a field that is night-blue under nothing. The campgrounds is the pairing to watch here the way the yurt and the burrow were last time: both are outdoors, both are dark, both are green. What keeps them apart is structural. The field is bare and open with the sky still on it and posts standing alone on the ground; this has a roof, and nothing in it stands alone because everything overlaps something. The field routes its lettering like a park sign, flat and incised; this sets a face whose strokes swell as they turn, because a rainforest is the one place where growing and thickening are the same verb. You are outside in one and inside the other. Every screen is a leaf — two pointed corners, two round ones, the same silhouette on the card and on the aperture, and the player is clipped into it when the button becomes an iframe. It is the reason thirty-odd rectangles of video do not read as a spreadsheet. The contrast checker found the canopy. The band of leaves across the top measured 2.18 against the ground behind it — a smudge, with no telling one leaf from another. WCAG does not reach ambient decoration and it was measured anyway, for the reason the Arcade’s quills were: a canopy nobody can make out is not a canopy, it is a dark strip pretending to be one. All three greens went up. Twenty-six new pairs, and every ink is held against the lit ground as well as the dark one, because the shafts land where they land and a word that only clears in the shade is a word somebody reads in the one place it fails. The light got a layer of its own, and the second reason is the one that mattered. Painted on the text column it stopped at the column’s edges and drew a hard bright line across the page under the canopy — a shaft with a lid on it. But at MAX the light shifts, and whatever carries the light is what fades: on the column, MAX GLITTER would have dimmed every word in the room by a tenth, twice a minute, in a room built for people who came here to stop being asked to work. The share card broke the fit checker, and the fix was in the checker. make-og.py measures where ink lands and refused this card for a crop that does not exist: the canopy’s leaves hang off both sides of their band and are clipped by it, so their boxes run past the edge while nothing is painted there. It skips descendants of a clipping <svg> now — reading the computed overflow rather than assuming it, so this stays a statement about paint — which is the same narrow exclusion check-gentle.py makes for transforms inside a drawing. It also caught a real one on the way: width: 100% resolves against the padding box, so the band’s negative right margin moved nothing and left a visible step 60px in from the edge of the card. Two new faces, and the room is the reason. Yeseva One and Cabin, self-hosted and OFL like everything else here. Cabin is a variable font, so one file is stored and declared twice against the weight axis — the same as Nunito.

item.title: a burrow under the street, and three class names that were already taken
item.description: The Latibulum is open. A door on the street that goes down into a hill: round door, lamp, thick walls, a wireless with one station on it, a tube television with one programme, and a shelf of things to do with a bodymind. Ryan’s brief, and his word. The word does both jobs already. Latibulum is Latin, and Lewis and Short give it as “a hiding-place, lurking-hole, covert, den, of animals” before giving the figurative sense and quoting Cicero calling a place the latibulum et perfugium doloris mei — the hiding-place and refuge of his grief. Ryan met it in a Walkabout Saga post; the room checks the sense against the dictionary rather than restating the post, so the two can be read against each other. In our own vocabulary it is a cave, the quiet end of a Cavendish Space, which is what stops it being a theme. It is the second warm brown room on this street, and that is the whole design problem. The Faery Yurt is also candlelit, also earth-toned, also built to hold somebody — and “they are both cosy, so they should feel the same” is the subroom excuse in a woolly jumper. The thing keeping them apart is structural rather than decorative: the yurt reads cream on dark all the way down, and almost every word in the burrow sits dark on a lit plaster wall. One is a pitched column of canvas with lights strung across it; the other is dug into a hill and has no sky in it anywhere. Two new faces for the same reason — a planed slab and a rounded sans, because a smial is carpentry and the yurt is calligraphy. The wireless is Adriel’s and stays where he put it. Ocean Waves is by Adriel Jeremiah Wool, a Stimpunk, and he has given us permission to use it however we like. It is a press-to-play facade anyway, because a permission is not a reason to take a copy of somebody’s seventy-four-minute composition off its own shelf, and because this street does not host anything musical. It is also not a recording of the ocean and the room says so: Ryan’s own line calls it a fractal composition of the nature of the ocean, and knowing that before you press it changes what you do with it. The television is a class you can take lying down. Annette of Itstimefitness, 22:45, seated tai chi and qigong — Repulse Monkey, Parting the Horse’s Mane, Cloud Arms — chosen for our own Campfire Learn Together on somatic practice. Everything in it is seated and not as a modification: as the design. The shelf refuses to be a checklist. Stretch, flap, fidget, meditate, stim dance, body scan, eat, drink, pee — lifted from our own Bodymind Break, and not one of them is a button. No ticks, no streak, nothing that notices which ones you did. A shelf that kept score would have turned a bodymind break into a small unpaid job, which is what the break is a break from — the same argument the pebbling cabinet makes about tallies, arriving in a room with no game in it. MAX GLITTER, down here, is one lamp breathing. Nothing in the room rotates at any setting, so there was no tilt to reset; the single animation is an opacity change over nine seconds on the lamp flame. The room says that on its own face rather than leaving somebody to turn it up and wonder whether it worked. And then the interesting bug, which was in the stylesheet rather than in the room. This site is one love.css holding a set of worlds that share nothing, and a class name is global whatever section it is written in. Four of this room’s names were already taken:.scrawl belongs to the zine table,.shelf to the bookshelf in the Faery Yurt,.knob to the Arcade’s speed control, and.tagline to the street’s six-typeface masthead. Only one of them was visible — the burrow’s trail line came out in the zine’s Rock Salt, which is how it was noticed at all. The other three were quietly inheriting a timber gradient, a button’s border and display: flex from rooms on the other side of the file. So there is a checker for that now. check-classes.py refuses a class claimed by two rooms’ sections of love.css, and — the half that catches the.tagline case, where the stylesheet is innocent and the markup is not — refuses a page wearing a class name another room has claimed. It is the CSS twin of check-ids.py and exists for the same reason: the browser applies the winner and says nothing. A third check was written and thrown away: a class styled in love.css that nothing wears is real dead weight, and it cannot be told apart from a class a script builds through a helper, because svgEl('frond', …) in otterly.js puts a class on an element without the word class appearing near it. It reported seven drawings that are on the screen right now, and a checker that cries wolf is one people stop running. And it found three leaks that were already here, none of them new. Two rules belonging to the quantum room had been left stranded at the bottom of the file, after the print section, which is how the print section came to look like it was claiming.fringe; they are back in their own room..scrawl turned out to be worn by the zine table, issue #2 and Enid’s room while living inside the zine’s section — three rooms on one class makes it furniture whichever section it was typed in, so it moved to §4 rather than being renamed twice. And the Faery Yurt’s tagline had been quietly taking display: flex and a 940px max-width from the street’s masthead since the room shipped. That one is a class name and not a design decision, so it is.yurt-tagline now; nothing of Helen’s moved, and the room renders pixel for pixel as it did. The share card is two grounds. Earth at the top with the lamp on it and the round door drawn on it, a band of lit plaster along the foot carrying dark type. That inversion is the room rather than a flourish, and a card that left it out would be advertising a different room. New contrast pairs for both halves; the brass moved from #C28F3C to #E3BB6A because a knob measured 1.93 against the lightest of the three woods behind it — a knob you could not see on the cabinet it is screwed to. The burrow’s two facades are in check-jukebox.py. A room with two of them is exactly the size at which somebody decides a list is not worth adding to a checker, and a dead station in a room built for people who are already flat is the worst place on this street to find rot.

item.title: a pebbling cabinet, and the licence that decided what it could be
item.description: Penguin Pebbling is in the Arcade. A shore, pebbles on it, three neighbours with nests. Walk into something to pick it up, carry it over, press GIVE. Every gift is taken and every one gets something different said back, because giving is how you find out who somebody is rather than a lock to pick. The first thing to say is that there is already a Penguin Pebbling game, and this is not it. Penguin Pebbling is thirty cards across all five locutions, by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, 2026, with Helen’s artwork. Go and play that one. The cabinet takes nothing from it — no cards, no prompts, no artwork, no five-locution structure. And the reason is a licence rather than modesty, which is worth writing down because it nearly was not noticed. The deck is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. This site is CC BY-SA 4.0, with no non-commercial clause. An adaptation would have dragged NC onto a page that cannot carry it; share-alike means it could not be quietly absorbed; and relicensing is not ours alone to do, because half the authorship and all the artwork are Helen’s. So the cabinet is built on the locution — coined by Amythest Schaber (Neurowonderful), documented by Stimpunks in 2022, written up by Helen at Autistic Realms in 2023 — which belongs to the community. Two of our own things with two different licences is exactly the case attribution exists for, and it is the first time on this site that a licence has changed what a page is rather than what it says at the bottom. It refuses a count, and that is the locution rather than a difficulty setting. No tally of what you gave, no total, no streak, nothing at the end. The neighbours bring you things on their own clock whether or not you have ever given them anything — built as a timer rather than as a reward, because a gift that arrives because you gave first is a trade. A number beside a practice that is explicitly not about volume would quietly make it about volume. The pale screen is the only one on the street, and the contrast work is why the pebbles have shapes. Everything on a shingle beach is a mid-tone including the shingle, so nothing on this screen is carried by its fill: every pebble, penguin and nest is drawn with the same dark outline, and check-contrast.py measures that outline against the three grounds and then each fill against the outline. That is the honest reading of WCAG 1.4.11, which asks about adjacent colours rather than about a fill against a distant background. But holding the fills to 4.5 against the outline squeezes them all light — and a narrow band of light tones is a narrow band of things nobody can tell apart. So the six things you can carry are six different shapes: a round pebble, a smooth one, a shard of sea glass, a speckled stone, a feather, a broken shell. Shape carries it, and the name said out loud on every pick-up carries it again. Thirteen new pairs, 195 in the file, none failing. The card inverts too, and had to. Gold on a pale sky measures 1.9, so the type is dark on light — the only share card on this street that is. It was decided by a measurement rather than chosen. A duplicate id, and a bug that would have been much worse anywhere else. The penguin’s drawing sits in the page’s <defs> as #peng and the player’s sprite was also id="peng", so getElementById returned the definition and the game threw on the first line of start(). It took thirty seconds to find because pressing START does something visible. The same mistake in markup nobody presses would have sat there, which is why the other cabinets’ cloned sprites were built out of <use> against one definition in the first place. All four arcade pages were swept; no others. So there is a checker for that now, and it immediately found a worse one. check-ids.py refuses a page that uses an id twice, and refuses a script that asks by name for an id no page loading it has. Run against the whole site it turned up seven elements sharing id="yurt-says" in the Faery Yurt — make-yurt-sound.py had been emitting a live region inside every sound tile, so six of them were dead markup that had never received a word, and love.js only ever reached the first. It had been live since the regulation nook shipped and nothing had said so, because a duplicate in markup nobody presses does not announce itself. The generator emits one shared region now. Broken on purpose with both real bugs put back; it named both. Two things found by looking at the screen rather than by any check. Every penguin was the same size on the same line, so there was no telling which one you were steering — the neighbours are drawn smaller and staggered up the beach now, and you are the one in front. And the nests were single filled ellipses that read as puddles the penguins were standing in; a nest is a rim with a hollow, which is also what the animal actually builds. And an honest note about the penguins, on the page. Adélie and gentoo penguins do build nests of stones, carry them about, and steal them from each other. The tidy romance — one penguin choosing the perfect pebble for its beloved — is the popular retelling rather than the finding. The locution is named after the image and is not weakened by that. A metaphor does not have to be a finding. There is no stealing in the cabinet, because the game is about the locution and not about penguins.

item.title: a second cabinet in the Arcade, in which floating gets you nothing
item.description: Otterly Adorbs. You steer an otter round a kelp bay. It twirls, somersaults, dives and floats on its back; three other otters keep their own rhythms; fish come through at feeding time and go again. Ryan’s proposal, and the name is his. It turned out not to be a blank sheet, which changed the design. The Stimpunks Solidarity Session has been leaving an otter cam running every Saturday for months — cameras on or off, some speaking, some in text, nobody has to watch. Helen Edgar wrote down what that was doing for her in Stimpunks Solidarity and Otters, and Star Stuff built The Stone You Keep (No. 58) on top of it, sourced to the primary literature. So the cabinet is built out of findings rather than out of charm, and otterly.js names the paper beside each one. Floating fills nothing up, and that is the single sharpest constraint in the build. No meter, no stamina, no bonus afterwards — the cabinet says so out loud the first time you roll over. Zine No. 58 refuses rest so you can produce in as many words: the otter is not recharging in order to forage better tomorrow. The friendly version of this game rewards resting, and the friendly version would have put a sentence on this page that another of our pages spends a spread refusing. It is written into CLAUDE.md so the next well-meant improvement gets stopped. A clam takes between 6 and 88 presses, and those are the real numbers. Two observers at Point Lobos in 1964 watched thirty instances over six days: a mussel took a mean of 35.5 blows, range 6 to 88 (Hall & Schaller). The game rolls in that range unrounded and reports your number with no target beside it. The urchin opens in a couple of goes and a stone does not help with it, which is Law et al. 2024 — some otters never carry one, because they are on the prey that does not need one, and the ones who do carry one keep their teeth. Nothing ranks the other three otters. Under food limitation a real population does not converge on one best way to be an otter; it fans out into specialists, each measurably better at its own thing (Tinker, Bentall & Estes, 2008). One of ours mostly floats, one mostly dives, one mostly turns in circles, and there is no scoreboard for any of it. The kelp does the holding. Float in the fronds and you stay where you are; float in open water and you drift. That is co-regulation stated as physics rather than as a metaphor, and it is the one mechanic that is also the reason the Saturday session works. It follows the zine’s correction rather than our own changelog. stimpunks.org’s week-28 entry describes the otter keeping “a favorite stone tucked in a pouch of skin” and returning to it “again and again”. No. 58 went to the primary and found the lifelong favourite rock in an armpit pouch is a popular retelling; what Hall & Schaller support is a stone kept and reused across successive food items within a bout of feeding. The game does the second thing. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins. A twirl is drawn frames, not a rotation, and that cost real work. Rotating the sprite would have been three lines — and would have made the room’s own comment false, because check-gentle.py reads rotation out of the computed matrix and this room says in its stylesheet that there is nothing there to read. So the otter has five drawn poses and a trick is a run through them. The angled poses are rotated, inside their own <svg>, where a transform is part of the picture the way a path’s d is. Frame-swapping is also what an actual cabinet did. The contrast checker found the seabed. It measured 1.10 against the water above it — invisible — and lightening the floor until it cleared 3:1 started swallowing the cobbles and the urchin that sit on it, which are the things a player reaches for. So the boundary is carried by a line instead, at 8.44 on the water and 9.25 on the bed. The information is “here is the floor”, and a line carries it perfectly well. Nineteen new pairs; 182 in the file, none failing. Buoyancy was winning an argument the player was trying to have with a clam. An otter is buoyant, so doing nothing takes you up — at the first setting that was about eight per cent of the bay a second, and it pulled you off the bed before you could pick a stone up. It is a quarter of that now, and it stops entirely while you are working on a shell, because an otter cracking something is holding itself there. Then the room split, and the share card is what decided it. Both games lived on one page for about an hour. Which meant a link to the otter game unfurled as a picture of a porcupine — the exact fault make-og.py exists to refuse, being committed by a room against its own second game. The Arcade is a foyer now, with the cabinets standing in it under lit marquees, and Quill Drift and Otterly Adorbs are pages with a machine on each. Three cards where there was one, and the two new ones are the screens: a flat dark field with Esmx and loose quills, and a kelp bay with an otter on its back. Those three pages share a carpet, a marquee, a cabinet build and a pixel face, and that is correct here. On this street that normally reads as the tidying instinct winning, so it is written into CLAUDE.md before somebody either “fixes” the similarity or cites it as licence to harmonise actual rooms. An arcade is precisely a room whose machines share a body and differ behind the glass. The worlds here are the screens, and a dark field and a kelp bay have nothing to do with each other. The chrome moved to a.arcade class so that the thing which styles and the thing which unfurls are never the same word — each page carries exactly one class make-og.py has a card for, and no ordering inside a class attribute decides anything. Each cabinet carries its own panels, its own refusals and its own credits. A single shared sidebar stopped working the moment there were two machines: a readout headed YOUR ESMX floating above an otter game is furniture belonging to nobody. The foyer keeps only what is true of every machine in the room — no timer, nothing chasing you, no sound, no memory, nothing moving until you press start. check-counts.py gained cabinets and games while this shipped and immediately refused two sentences calling one of them “the second cabinet”.

item.title: the street stops saying how many rooms it has, and a checker to keep it that way
item.description: Ryan’s call: the number of storefronts is going to grow well past anything worth writing down, so nothing here states a total any more. Not the pages, not the stylesheet’s comments, not a generator’s published strings, not the docs. The street’s own description, its share card, llms.txt, the feed’s description, the liner notes, the campground’s lede and the empty storefront’s opening line all say something that stays true however many there are — no two rooms alike, one card per room, a row of shopfronts, a storefront with nothing in it. The change that opened the Arcade is the argument for this, and it is not a flattering one. That commit carefully updated the room count in twelve places — and shipped three sentences still carrying the old one. love.css went on describing the doors and the shopfronts by a number that had stopped being true the moment the seventh one landed, and CLAUDE.md went on giving the number of share-card designs as one fewer than existed. All three were written by the same session that was updating the other twelve, and nothing caught them, because nothing was looking. A total is a fact about the whole site that gets written in a dozen places and updated in one. So check-counts.py refuses a number or an ordinal sitting in front of a thing that grows when a storefront opens — rooms, storefronts, shopfronts, doors, worlds, card designs. It is deliberately small. The jukebox’s tracks and The Chappell’s are real counts of real data, generated from files holding exactly that many, and it leaves them alone. It starts at four, because the first draft refused its own fix. Written to catch any number from two upwards, the very first thing it flagged was “no two rooms alike” — the count-free phrasing this whole change exists to encourage — along with “two rooms turned out to be putting text on a background nobody had measured”, which is a finding rather than a claim about the size of the street. Below four, a number in front of these nouns is nearly always counting instances. A street’s total will be four and rising. Quoted text is skipped in prose and not in code, and the asymmetry is the point. A page or a doc has to be able to say what it corrected, so a count inside quotation marks there is evidence rather than a claim. In a generator every quoted string is a candidate for publication — make-og.py writes its card footers out of string literals — so there is no safe quotation, and the checker’s own docstring therefore describes the three stale counts rather than quoting them. It is the one place where a tool’s prose has to obey the rule it enforces. The first version scanned line by line and refused itself, because the quotation it makes its argument out of wrapped across two. Broken on purpose in all three shapes that actually shipped — a page’s prose (“the seventh storefront”), a stylesheet comment (“the six doors”) and a generator’s docstring (“eleven card designs”) — and it named all three with their file and line. Then the working tree was put back. One count it missed on the way, which is why it grew a word. The Arcade’s own source said the room “shares nothing with the six next door”, and the first rule sailed past it because next was not in the short list of words allowed to sit between a number and its noun. It is in the list now, and the sentence says the rooms next door. The share card changed with the street. Its footer read ONE STREET · SEVEN ROOMS · A FIELD PAST THE TREELINE and now reads NO TWO ROOMS ALIKE, which is the better line anyway: the count was never the interesting claim, and the thing it was standing in for is the one this site is actually about. The room numbers on the doors stay. room 04, room 05, ROOM 07 are addresses, and a house number has never told anybody how long the street is.

item.title: the second yell, and a duration that lies about itself
item.description: The yell button has two voices in it. The Playhouse holds a yell from Enigma, lent on 2026-09-20 — the first on that button from somebody other than the person who built the room. It is published under the name it came with, the room says whose yell it was out loud on the press, and it is credited in the liner notes as well. It carries no onward licence, unlike everything else here: CC BY-SA cannot be revoked, and a voice somebody lends us has to be one they can take back. Two tools refused it on arrival, which is what they are for. The file sat in audio/yells/ with no entry in data/yells.json, so make-yells.py stopped — a yell with nobody’s name on it is the one thing it cannot publish — and make-yurt-sound.py’s sweep of every audio file in the repo stopped on the metadata: com.apple, Core Media, and a creation timestamp to the second. Neither tool strips anything, and that is deliberate: what to do with somebody’s recording is theirs to decide, not a script’s. It was stripped once there was a decision to strip it. And the obvious way to check that strip is misleading. The instruction in both docstrings is to compare the duration before and after, because -c copy re-muxes rather than re-encodes. It went from 4.160s to 4.096s — 64 milliseconds apparently gone, which reads exactly like a bad edit. It is not. -map_metadata -1 drops the iTunSMPB tag, which is the container’s declaration of encoder padding, and the start offset went 0.044 to 0.000 with it. Decoding both files to raw PCM gives 196,608 samples each, identical at every one of them, same peak. The audio is untouched; the 64ms was never audio. Written down here because the check the tools recommend will keep producing that number, and the next person to run it should not go looking for what they cut off. The house rule rewrote itself, which is the whole reason it is generated. The Playhouse now says the button holds “2 recorded yells” rather than one. A claim a page makes about itself should not depend on somebody remembering to edit it. Verified in the network panel afterwards: zero requests to audio/ on load, one per press, and both names reached the live region.

item.title: a seventh storefront, with one cabinet in it
item.description: The street has an arcade on it. The Arcade is room seven, sixth door in the row, and it holds one game: Quill Drift, starring Esmx the Porkypine. Loose quills drift across a dark field, Esmx walks, and a quill joins the mane on contact and only on contact. No timer, no lives, no score, no streak, nothing chasing anybody and no way to lose a quill once it is in. The one rule is the mechanic, not a note at the bottom of it. A porcupine cannot shoot a quill — cannot throw, fire or launch one; it comes away in whatever touched it, and an attacker has to come to the animal. That is card No. 3 of the Quillery, sourced there to Uldis Roze. A spiky mascot invites precisely the opposite reading, so the game has no verb for it: there is nothing to aim, nothing to press but a direction, and nothing on the field but Esmx and the quills. “Non-violent” was the brief; refusing the one verb everybody expects is what it turned into. The point of the game is a variant, which is what the licence asks for. Twelve quills fill the mane, and what you are left with is a mane in an order nobody else walked into — written out in words beside the cabinet as well as drawn on the sprite, because a mane nobody can read is a mane nobody can tell anybody about. Esmx’s own page does not merely permit this: feel free to customise! Make variants of Esmx to represent your community. A correction, caught by Ryan mid-build and worth the space. The room shipped its first draft calling Esmx “our mascot and not ours”, and borrowed the framing from the Quillery, which says Kaya Oldaker’s artwork “is not ours to redraw stroke for stroke”. That is wrong about the facts. Stimpunks commissioned Esmx and holds the IP; Kaya is the artist. The credit line stays on every surface it was on — in the room, in the liner notes and in the drawing’s own markup — because holding the rights to a commission is not a reason to stop naming the hand that drew it, which is a different and better sentence than the one that was there. Attribution here is a courtesy as well as a licence, and it turns out the courtesy is the half that was doing the work. Esmx is drawn again rather than pasted in, and not because anybody needed permission. The originals are a download away and ours to use. A PNG would have been the only thing in the arcade that came from somewhere else, in a room whose whole argument is that it shares nothing with the six next door — and taking our own invitation seemed like the least we could do with it. The marks that make Esmx Esmx are kept: the pig snout, the earring in one ear, the chunk out of the other, and a mane that comes apart at the tips. An arcade in particular, because the mascot already came from one. Kaya’s notes say Esmx resembles a Sonic character or a Pokémon on purpose, due to their popularity within the Autistic community. Nothing of either is used here. The room is not a costume put on the mascot; it is where the mascot came from. The dial and the speed knob are two controls, on purpose. The dial governs the room — the cabinet glow, the marquee bulbs — and the game’s speed belongs to the player. The dial picks the knob’s starting position, Slow if you arrived on Gentle, and then stops having an opinion; all three speeds are offered at every dial setting. Tying the game to the dial would have made Gentle a different game, which is the “lite version” mistake with a joystick on it. And nothing on the playfield moves until a coin goes in — the jukebox’s consent model in a different costume, and the reason a room with a game in it does not make the dial lie. Motion the visitor started is not ambient motion. The cabinet also makes no sound at all, ever, at any setting; an arcade that is silent by choice seemed better than one that is silent until it isn’t. Everything moves with left / top, and that is a decision about the checker rather than about performance. Rotation and skew are what check-gentle.py reads out of the computed matrix, and a room that put its game behind a transform would be asking that tool to take the room’s word for something. There is nothing to take on trust if there is no transform to read. The two that are there are the sprite’s centring translate and a scaleX(-1) when Esmx turns round — both of which the tool already reads as layout, and both of which it can see. Broken on purpose with an unreset rotate(-2deg) on the cabinet marquee: it named p.cab-marquee and the matrix it found. 192 elements in the room, measured at all three settings, none tilting. Thirty-six new contrast pairs, two of them against grounds nobody chose. #0F1F24 is what the screen becomes under its scanline stripe and is the lighter of the two grounds the playfield makes, so it is the one that decides; #2D1C25 is the carpet under the cabinet’s own glow, where the headline and the eyebrow sit. The eight quills are in the list too — WCAG 1.4.3 does not reach a graphic, but a quill you cannot pick out of the background is a control you cannot use, and they are held to the body threshold rather than the 3:1 one so that nobody has to remember later which bar applied. Each quill also has a name, said out loud on contact, because colour is never the only channel here. 162 pairs, none failing; broken on purpose by dimming one grey, and the composite ground failed harder than the flat one, which is the whole argument for having both in the file. make-og.py refused the room until it had a card, which is exactly what it is for — the eleventh design, and the one that is mostly a drawing, because this is the only room whose subject is a character rather than an argument and a poster for a game showing nobody playing it would be a poster for the wrong thing. Esmx and the marquee bulbs are lifted out of the page rather than retyped, alongside the campground’s stream and the yurt’s crown, so the card cannot come to disagree with the room. The mane on it is the markup’s own default rainbow; the game only ever overwrites those twelve fills with what a player actually caught. Press Start 2P is the eighteenth family and the only face in the room. A pixel face is the one thing no other room on this street could have borrowed without turning into the arcade. 4.7KB, latin only, self-hosted like the other seventeen — verified in the network panel: every byte on the page comes from this origin, and the cabinet fetches nothing when you press anything, because there is nothing to fetch. Playtested, and the first build was over before its own instructions were. Six quills on the field at a reach of 7.5 filled a twelve-quill mane in about ten seconds. Dropping to five at 6.2 went too far the other way — a full lap of the field turned up one quill and the game went slack. Six at 7.0 fills a mane in something under a minute of walking, measured over a sixteen-leg random walk rather than guessed. “Six rooms” was written down in twelve places — the street’s description and its card alt, llms.txt, love.css’s own header, the liner notes, the campground’s lede, the feed’s description and the street card’s footer. It is seven now, and Your Room is the seventh storefront rather than the sixth. The derived files are derived, so make-sitemap.py and make-feed.py carried their own copies of the sentence and had to be edited at the source rather than in the output. The pad takes a press-and-hold or a single click, because a control that only works while a button is held down is not a control for somebody driving it with a switch or a screen reader. The arrow keys are bound to the playfield rather than to the document — arrow keys that stop the page scrolling from anywhere on it would be a trap — and Escape hands them back.

item.title: a checker for the dial, and the windowsill it caught
item.description: The dial had nothing watching it. check-gentle.py loads all fourteen pages in headless Chrome, sets the intensity to Gentle, Regular and MAX GLITTER in turn, and reads what actually moves out of 2,253 computed styles — rather than reading the stylesheet and believing it. The global half was always safe: animation and transition are killed at Gentle with!important, and nothing out-shouts that by accident. The tilts were never safe. Every room sets its own rotations and resets them room by room, unprefixed, so a reset is one selector away from being outranked — and CSS does not warn when that happens. It applies the winner and says nothing. It found the Faery Yurt’s windowsill on its first run. A book at rotate(-3deg) and a pen at rotate(24deg), both still tilted for anybody who had asked the wobble to stop, because that room shipped without a single Gentle rule in it. Twenty-four degrees is not subtle. The room was a day old and two people had read it. The sill keeps its angles at Regular and MAX — they are Helen’s and they stay; the reset is the dial, which is our plumbing and applies to every room on the street. Rotation and skew are the wobble; a mirror and a translate are not. The tool reads the off-diagonal terms of the computed matrix, which are non-zero for exactly those two and nothing else, so a vine flipped with scaleX(-1) and a positioned layer pass without needing an exception. Transforms inside an <svg> are excluded on purpose: a transform on a <g> is part of the drawing, the same kind of thing as a path’s d, and flattening one would produce a broken picture rather than a calmer page. It checks the other half of the sentence too. “Never the words” means the visible text of a page has to be identical at Gentle and at Regular. It is, on all fourteen — which is the moment to write the check, rather than after somebody has a paragraph they would rather drop at the quiet setting. Broken on purpose three times before being believed, because a checker that has only ever passed is a checker nobody has tested. Restoring the near-miss on Enid’s wall — the tilt selector written one level too specific — and it names figure.polaroid. Hiding a.scrawl at Gentle and it reports the pages whose word count drops. Leaving an!important animation running and it names the element. Then the working tree was put back.

item.title: the wall becomes a wall, and a tilt that nearly outranked the dial
item.description: Enid’s photographs were stacking in a single narrow column, and the prose panel beside them was being stretched to match: 1,291 pixels of bordered box holding 218 pixels of writing, and 1,073 of nothing. The row they sat in never carried align-items, so it defaulted to stretch — and the row one level up already had flex-start, which is the tell that this was an omission rather than a decision. It was correct the day it was written and rotted as the site succeeded. With the wall grey, the column was one note at 222px and the panel was 218px; stretch looked like alignment. Every photograph anybody sent added about 350px of emptiness to the panel next door, because aspect-ratio: auto is the no-crop promise and a portrait renders at full portrait height. The third photo is what made it impossible to miss. Nothing would have reported this — it is not a failing check, it is a room that looks slightly wrong and gets slightly wronger. So the wall is a wall now: sticker wall, then photographs across it, then the prose underneath. Polaroids are one fixed size, the way real ones are, and they pack across and wrap — the tenth photograph widens the wall instead of lengthening the page. Heights stay ragged, because the frame still adapts to each picture. Simulated eight photos in the page to watch it wrap: 3 / 3 / 2, the short last row staying short rather than stretching one polaroid to full width. The page is 1,175px where it was 2,860. Every other photograph leans the other way, because three in a row all tilted -2deg reads as one skewed strip rather than three separately pinned pictures. And that tilt nearly turned the wobble back on for the people who turned it off. The obvious selector —.polaroid-wall.polaroid:nth-child(even) — is specificity (0,3,0), and the Gentle reset is html[data-intensity="gentle"].polaroid at (0,2,1). The decoration would have outranked the dial, in the one room whose photographs are of real people, and nothing here checks computed transforms so it would have shipped silently. It is written:where(.polaroid-wall).polaroid:nth-child(even)::where() contributes no specificity, which holds the rule at (0,2,0) and under the reset. Read the computed transform at all three settings rather than trusting the arithmetic — Regular and MAX GLITTER tilt −2°, +1.5°, −2°; Gentle is none, none, none. The generator moved two spaces and learned nothing else. make-polaroids.py writes the wall between its markers and has no opinion about the container, so the restructure was ours to make; only its indentation changed, to match the new depth. Re-ran it against the rebuilt room and the output is byte-identical, which is the property that matters — the next photograph has to land in a row, not quietly restore the column.

item.title: the regulation nook makes noises, and a hole between three tools
item.description: The Regulation Nook makes noises. All six of Helen’s tiles in the Faery Yurt are buttons now — blankets, squishmallows, fairy lights, cupcakes, coffee, cheese and pesto — and each plays a couple of seconds of Ryan making the appropriate noise. An easter egg Ryan and Helen wanted in her room. Each sound owns exactly one marker pair in the page and nothing else, rather than the tool generating the whole list: a tile whose recording is withdrawn goes back to being Helen’s own markup, and that has to be a change to one tile rather than a rewrite of six. An easter egg that still tells you it is there. A tile with a sound wears the same candlelit card as its neighbours, and a small ♪ 2s surfaces on hover and on focus; the button’s accessible name says it is a sound and how long. The discovery is meant to be “one of these is a button”, not “a page I was reading quietly made a noise at me” — a hidden noise would be the exact thing the dial and the press-to-play facades exist to prevent, arriving as a joke. At Gentle the marker is simply always shown, because the quiet setting should reveal more and never less. Nothing is fetched until you press. Verified in the network panel: zero requests to audio/ on load, one per press, and never two playing at once — pressing a second tile is a change of mind, not two people talking over each other. Whose voice it is is said out loud into a live region on every press rather than only filed in the liner notes, where it is also filed. Every runtime is measured off the file, not typed. The six labels say 2, 2, 3, 2, 4 and 2 seconds because that is what the containers report. Every press-to-play control on this street promises a duration before the press — the jukebox, the thirteen arches, the audio room’s sequence — and a hand-kept number is a promise one edit away from being false. Then the interesting part: three tools guarding audio, and a hole between them. make-readings.py refuses stray recorder metadata on passages, make-yells.py on yells, and the new tool on the yurt’s — and every one of them only ever looked at files its own data file named. Recordings sat in audio/ for an afternoon carrying com.apple.VoiceMemos (iPad Version 26.6.2), a creation timestamp to the second and a voice-memo UUID, belonging to no tool’s patch, one git add -A from being permanent in a public repository. make-yurt-sound.py now walks every audio file in the repo instead. Three guards with a hole between them is a hole. It refuses rather than strips. What to do with somebody’s recording is theirs to decide, and a tool that silently rewrote the files people dropped in would be worse than one that says what is wrong and names the file.

item.title: the third photograph, and the promise it broke on arrival
item.description: Helen sent her portrait, for both places at once. It is on Enid’s wall and it is the picture beside the welcome in her own room — the empty slot the yurt shipped with two commits ago, because the file was not ours to invent. Description, caption and naming are hers, and she took it herself. No EXIF, not resized, not cropped. And not filtered, which is the part worth writing down. Her mockup put a sepia wash over this photograph — filter: sepia(.18) saturate(1.05) brightness(.96) — and the terms promise, in these words, that we will not “Crop you. Filter you.” A promise the site makes to everybody is not waived by the one person it happens to be about this time, because the next photograph would arrive under a rule that had already been bent once. The wooden frame is matting and stays: a border, a shadow or a mat goes around a picture; a filter is done to it. So the tool checks it rather than trusting anybody to remember. make-polaroids.py now refuses a filter in an ’s own style attribute, and refuses any rule in love.css whose selector reaches a photograph and carries one. Every photograph on the site wears class="photo" so there is something exact to look for. The first version of that check did not work, and the way it failed is the point. It scanned only the classes on the itself, so it sailed straight past.portrait-frame img { filter: … } — the filter was on a descendant selector, which is the shape this actually arrives in. It was written, it passed, and it was wrong; it only got caught because putting the sepia back and watching the tool say nothing is cheaper than believing it. A checker that passes a case it was built for is worse than no checker, and this one nearly shipped as exactly that. All three shapes refuse now — descendant selector, the plate’s own class, and an inline style — each one tested by breaking it on purpose.

item.title: the street grows an edge, and Helen pitches a yurt on it
item.description: There is a signpost at the end of the shopfronts now. The Campgrounds — a field past the treeline with numbered pitches on it, for the people who do not want a storefront. A row of lit shops is a wonderful place to be and an exhausting place to live, and a site that only had one of those was telling its own quiet people that the loud room is the only room. The signpost is deliberately not a seventh door: a door here is a shop you walk into, and this is where the street stops. Nothing in the field moves at any setting — not at Gentle, not at Regular, not at MAX GLITTER. Every other page has an ambient layer waiting for the dial to be turned up; this one has none, and says so on the page. An area that exists for people who want quiet cannot have a loud setting and mean it. The dial still governs each pitch, which are their own worlds and set their own noise. Pitch 01 is the Faery Yurt, and it is Helen Edgar’s room rather than ours. The palette, the three typefaces, the drawings, the twelve book spines, the shutters on the glimmer window and every line of copy came from a mockup she built and sent. We added the plumbing and changed one colour. It is credited to her in the liner notes, in a section that did not exist until there was a room by somebody else to put in it. The yurt shares nothing with the field it is pitched on, and that was the hardest version of this rule yet. The Chappell at least had a parent room to differ from; this is the first thing in a brand new area, where “an area should look like an area” is the most reasonable-sounding sentence the tidying instinct has produced here since “it is only a subroom”. The field is cold blue spruce, bone signs routed like park lettering, and bare ground. The yurt is candlelit brown, old serifs and soft cards. You walk in out of the night air; the contrast is the door. They got a share card each, ninth and tenth, for the same reason. The contrast checker caught two things in Helen’s mockup before it shipped. Her smallest grey, #8a7462, carries the eyebrow, the shelf note, the window hint, the animal cards and the footer — and it measures 4.30 on the flat tent ground, 3.85 on a card and 3.43 under the ember glow, failing everywhere it is used. It is #A4907B now. Her fourth book spine ran to #9a6c2f, where the cream lettering measured 3.74; it stops at #8A5F26. Thirty-nine new pairs, including one against #31231A — a colour nobody wrote, which is what the yurt’s canvas weave and ember crown actually composite to. 126 pairs, none failing. This is the only thing about her room this site changed, and it is written down rather than quietly applied. The consent record now guards every page, not just the wall. The yurt hangs one of Enid’s photographs in Helen’s own room, which put the consent record and the publication in two different places for the first time — exactly the gap where a withdrawal gets half-honoured. make-polaroids.py walks all the HTML now: a photo published anywhere without an entry is a refusal, a photo hung outside the wall without that entry saying so is a refusal, and a file sitting in photos/ with no record at all is a refusal. Delete a withdrawn entry and the tool refuses to run until the yurt lets go of it too, instead of leaving a broken image on a page nobody thought to check. Five typefaces arrived at once, which is what it costs to open an area whose two pages share nothing with the street or with each other. Alfa Slab One and Bitter are the campground’s routed sign and its field notice; Cormorant Garamond, Crimson Pro and Caveat are Helen’s, named in her own mockup. All five are self-hosted, so the yurt still makes no third-party request — verified in the network panel, along with the field: every byte on both pages comes from this origin. A keyboard fix the mockup could not have caught. The glimmer window’s shutters are opened by a visually hidden checkbox, so the site’s focus ring was landing on something invisible and a keyboard visitor had no way to tell they were on it. The ring goes on the window frame now.

item.title: the second photograph
item.description: Enid’s wall has somebody else on it. Helen Edgar, on a grand staircase — the first photograph up there from somebody other than the person who built the room, which is the difference between a process and a person waving his own picture through. The description and the caption are the words it arrived with, because the terms do not allow any other kind. The photographer is credited without being named. A friend took it and would rather stay anonymous, and the permission is on the record anyway — the tool refuses a credited photographer with no permission logged, and anonymous is a way of being named rather than a way of skipping the question. Being in a picture is not the same as owning it. Checked before publishing, not promised: no EXIF, so no location data left on the file; the photograph keeps its own shape, because the plate stopped cropping when the first one went up; and it carries no onward licence, so it comes down the day she says so and nobody else gets to reuse it in the meantime.

item.title: a door at the back of the dancefloor
item.description: Pink Pony Club has a subroom. The Chappell — thirteen Chappell Roan videos under the heading Unabashed Pleasure and Righteous Inclusion, which is the name of a playlist we already published. The room argues that the two halves of that title are usually kept apart, that Disabled people get handed the righteous one and told the other is a reward for good behaviour, and that unabashed pleasure is not the opposite of inclusion but what inclusion is for. Rhinestone Vatican, and it shares nothing with its parent. The dancefloor is flat hot pink, cream Shrikhand and ten small white cards inside one big cream tray. This is votive indigo, gold Monoton, and thirteen free-standing arches with stained glass over each one, standing on the bare ground. A subroom is the place where inheriting the parent’s look would have seemed most reasonable, which is exactly why it does not — and it got its own share card for the same reason, the eighth. Monoton was the last unclaimed display face on the street. It held one 27px line on the index, “Living out loud”, and no room had taken it as a headline. A neon marquee face set in gold leaf is the whole joke of this room in one typeface. Every button says how long before you press it. There is a twenty-three minute Tiny Desk concert in there sitting beside three-minute videos, and “press play” is only consent if you know what you are agreeing to — the same reasoning that put the passage count on the audio room’s sequence control. The generator refuses a track with no runtime rather than rendering a blank one, because a missing runtime would not look like a bug, it would look like a choice. Nothing was guessed.
